cards.front: What is the key difference between a workgroup and a Windows domain?
cards.back: Workgroup: each device manages its own credentials independently. Domain: one central Active Directory database manages all users, devices, and permissions.

cards.front: Which Windows editions can join an Active Directory domain?
cards.back: Pro, Enterprise, and Education. Windows Home cannot join a domain - the option is grayed out.

cards.front: Control Panel path to join a domain or workgroup?
cards.back: Control Panel > System > Change settings (or Settings > System > About > Domain or Workgroup > Change). Requires domain admin credentials.

cards.front: How do you create a hidden network share?
cards.back: Append a dollar sign ($) to the share name. Example: Data$ hides the share from browse lists but anyone who knows the UNC path can still connect.

cards.front: Name three built-in Windows administrative shares.
cards.back: ADMIN$, C$ (and other drive letters), IPC$. All hidden by default ($ suffix).

cards.front: Where in Windows can you view all currently shared folders?
cards.back: Computer Management > Shared Folders > Shares.

cards.front: Command to map a network drive to H: from the CLI?
cards.back:
net use H: \\server\share
For paths with spaces: net use H: "\\server\Gate Room"

cards.front: What does hiding a share ($ suffix) NOT do?
cards.back: It does not secure the share. Users who know the UNC path can still connect. Permissions are the only real access control.

cards.front: Three network profiles in Windows Defender Firewall?
cards.back: Private, Public, and Domain (appears only when the device is joined to an Active Directory domain).

cards.front: Which firewall profile is the most restrictive?
cards.back: Public. It blocks inbound connections and disables file sharing - intended for untrusted networks like coffee shops.

cards.front: Where do you create advanced inbound/outbound firewall rules?
cards.back: Windows Defender Firewall with Advanced Security (wf.msc). Right-click Inbound Rules > New Rule.

cards.front: What are the four rule types in the Windows Firewall New Rule wizard?
cards.back: Program, Port, Predefined, Custom.

cards.front: What are the three actions you can set on a Windows Firewall rule?
cards.back: Allow, Allow if secure (IPsec required), Block.

cards.front: What is APIPA and what IP range does it use?
cards.back: Automatic Private IP Addressing - a fallback when DHCP is unavailable. Range: 169.254.1.0 through 169.254.254.255. Also called link-local; no internet access.

cards.front: A device shows 169.254.x.x in ipconfig. What does this indicate?
cards.back: DHCP failed. The device fell back to APIPA. Check DHCP server availability and network connectivity.

cards.front: What is the loopback address and what does pinging it test?
cards.back: 127.0.0.1 (any 127.x.x.x). Pinging it tests the local TCP/IP stack without sending traffic to the network.

cards.front: Four required settings for any static IP configuration?
cards.back: IP address, subnet mask, default gateway, DNS server.

cards.front: What is the Alternate Configuration tab used for?
cards.back: Lets a device try DHCP first, then fall back to a specific static IP (instead of APIPA) if DHCP fails. Useful for laptops that roam between networks.

cards.front: What cipher does WPA2/WPA3 use? What cipher is WPA1 (legacy)?
cards.back: WPA2/WPA3 always use AES. WPA1 used TKIP (now deprecated/legacy).

cards.front: When a device has both wired Ethernet and Wi-Fi active, which takes traffic by default?
cards.back: Wired Ethernet. It has a lower metric (higher priority) and is always preferred when connected.

cards.front: What is a VPN concentrator?
cards.back: A corporate device that decrypts inbound VPN traffic from clients and forwards it to the internal network. The client encrypts; the concentrator decrypts.

cards.front: Settings path to set up a VPN connection in Windows?
cards.back: Network and Sharing Center > Set up a new connection > Connect to a workplace. Or Settings > Network and Internet > VPN.

cards.front: What is WWAN and how can it be connected?
cards.back: Wireless Wide Area Network - cellular data. Connected via built-in hardware adapter, USB modem, or smartphone tethering/hotspot.

cards.front: Two places to configure a proxy server in Windows?
cards.back: Control Panel > Internet Options > Connections > LAN Settings, OR Settings > Network and Internet > Proxy.

cards.front: What does marking a connection as 'metered' do in Windows?
cards.back: Reduces background data usage: throttles Windows Update downloads, OneDrive sync, and app updates. Useful for cellular hotspots or capped data plans.

cards.front: Where do you set a connection as metered?
cards.back: Settings > Network and Internet > [select the adapter] > Metered connection toggle.

cards.front: What network profile should you select when connecting at a coffee shop?
cards.back: Public. It disables file sharing and blocks inbound connections - correct for untrusted networks.

cards.front: WPA2 Enterprise vs WPA2 Personal - what is the authentication difference?
cards.back: Personal uses a pre-shared key (PSK - one password for all). Enterprise uses 802.1X with a RADIUS server for individual user authentication.
